The shipping container is a plain steel box, and almost everything interesting about it happened
outside the box. Before containers, a ship carried sacks, barrels, crates and loose bundles, and a
crew of dockworkers moved each item by hand between the quay and the hold. A cargo could sit in a
port for a week while men rearranged it. The cost of that week was invisible in the freight rate
and enormous in the total. When Malcom McLean converted a tanker to carry truck trailers in 1956,
the saving he found was not in the steel. It was in the hours that stopped being spent.

What made the box work was agreement. A container is useful only if the crane at the far end can
lift it, the truck chassis can carry it, and the railcar can take it without modification. That
means corner castings in the same place, the same lengths, the same stacking strength, everywhere.
The agreement took a decade of argument, and several shipping lines lost money defending sizes
that did not survive. The standard that emerged was not the best design anyone had drawn. It was
the one enough parties could live with.

Ports changed shape as a result. The old finger piers of Manhattan and Liverpool were built for
ships that stayed a long time and for warehouses that stood close to the water. A container port
wants the opposite: a straight quay, deep water, and a very large flat yard behind it. Cities that
had no room for the yard lost their traffic to places that did, often a short distance away and
usually with a cheaper workforce. Newark took New York's cargo. Felixstowe took London's.

Something similar happened to the crews. A ship that once needed two hundred dockers now needs a
crane driver, a lasher and a clerk. The union response is one of the better studied labour
conflicts of the century, partly because it ended in a bargain rather than a defeat: in several
ports the men accepted mechanisation in exchange for guaranteed income, and the guarantees were
honoured for decades.

Consider a different kind of system, with a similar lesson about interfaces. A wine region is
usually described by soil and weather, and both matter, but the thing that decides whether a
region has a reputation is a set of rules about what may be written on the label. Burgundy sells
place names. Bordeaux sells estate names. Champagne sells a method and a region together, and has
defended the pairing in court for a century. None of those choices follows from the chemistry of
the grape. They are commercial decisions that became traditions, and the tradition then shaped the
planting.

Soil does matter, though not in the way the marketing suggests. Vines do badly in rich ground.
Given plenty of water and nitrogen they grow leaves, set heavy crops, and make thin wine. The
famous slopes are famous partly because they are poor: stony, shallow, well drained, and steep
enough that water leaves quickly. A vine under mild stress sends roots down instead of shoots out,
and ripens a smaller crop more completely. The grower's craft is largely the management of that
stress, which is why the same clone planted two hundred metres apart can give two different wines.

Weather sets the outer limits. A late frost in May can remove most of a crop in one night, and the
countermeasures are all crude: burning straw, spraying water so that the latent heat of freezing
holds the buds at zero, or flying a helicopter low enough to mix the warm air above the inversion
into the cold layer below. Each of these is expensive, none is reliable, and all of them are used.

Bread is a third example of the same pattern, where a small number of physical facts are dressed
up as tradition. Wheat flour makes a dough that holds gas because two proteins, glutenin and
gliadin, form a network when hydrated and worked. Rye has much less of that network and relies on
pentosans instead, which is why rye bread is denser and why a rye dough is sticky rather than
elastic. Sourdough is not a flavour so much as an ecology: a stable community of lactic acid
bacteria and wild yeast, in which the bacteria outnumber the yeast by roughly a hundred to one and
set the acidity, while the yeast does most of the lifting.

The acidity does more than taste sour. It slows the enzymes that would otherwise degrade the
starch, it strengthens the gluten network at moderate levels and weakens it at high ones, and it
makes the loaf keep longer by discouraging the mould that would otherwise arrive on the third day.
Bakers learned all of this by feel long before anyone wrote down the mechanism, and the written
mechanism has not changed the practice much. It has mostly explained why the practice works.

Mountains give a fourth case, and here the timescale is what surprises people. The Alps are young,
which is why they are high and sharp; the Appalachians are old, which is why they are low and
rounded. But the rounding is not simple wear. A mountain range is a load on the crust, and the
crust floats. As erosion removes material from the top, the range rises in response, so the rocks
now at the summit were once several kilometres below the surface. A range can lose a vertical
kilometre of rock and end up only a few hundred metres shorter. The valleys deepen faster than the
peaks fall.

Glaciers cut differently from rivers, and the difference is visible from a train window. A river
cuts a V, because the water works at a line on the valley floor. A glacier cuts a U, because the
ice works across its whole width and plucks at the walls as well as the bed. Where a small glacier
joined a larger one, the small valley is left hanging above the big one, and a waterfall marks the
join. Yosemite is a catalogue of this, and so is the west coast of Scotland, where the sea has
since flooded the U-shaped valleys and made the sea lochs.

The last example is the one with the clearest economics. Salt was a strategic good for most of
recorded history, not because it is rare but because it is heavy and needed in quantity. Meat and
fish could not be kept through a winter without it. Places that could make salt cheaply, by
evaporating seawater in a warm dry climate or by pumping brine from a dome, sold it far inland at
prices set almost entirely by transport. Roads were named after it. Taxes were levied on it, and
the taxes were resented out of proportion to their size, because salt is one of the few goods that
a poor household cannot simply do without.

Refrigeration removed the strategic value in about forty years, and the industry that remained is
mostly chemical: chlorine, caustic soda, and the road salt that keeps winter traffic moving. The
tonnage is larger than it has ever been. The price is low enough that nobody thinks about it. That
is the usual fate of a commodity whose importance was really the importance of the problem it
solved, and the problem got solved another way.
